summary: Engadget's Andrew Tarantola looks back on ChatGPT's first year after its November 30, 2022 launch, covering record user growth, Microsoft's $10 billion investment, product updates, and the backlash it drew. The article walks through each quarter of 2023, including copyright lawsuits, bans, hallucination incidents, and the brief firing and return of Sam Altman. It concludes that ChatGPT looks unlikely to fade, though regulation may shape its future.
one_line: A quarter-by-quarter retrospective on ChatGPT's first year, covering record growth, Microsoft's investment, lawsuits, regulatory pushback and the Sam Altman firing drama.
key_facts: ChatGPT launched November 30, 2022 alongside GPT-3.5; OpenAI had been developing GPT since 2016, unveiling GPT-1 in 2018 and reaching GPT-3 by June 2020.
ChatGPT hit 100 million monthly active users in two months, faster than TikTok or Instagram and the fastest adoption to 100 million in internet history.
In January 2023 Microsoft extended its partnership with OpenAI with a $10 billion investment.
By February 2023 OpenAI was reportedly worth just under $30 billion, and ChatGPT was integrated into BingChat (now Copilot) and the Edge browser.
In March 2023 OpenAI announced the subscription service ChatGPT Plus and added plug-in and API support; ChatGPT also reached 100 million users per day, 30 times higher than two months earlier.
In March 2023 Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak and other AI researchers signed an open letter demanding a six month moratorium on AI development.
In April 2023 Italy banned ChatGPT use by public sector employees citing GDPR data privacy violations; the ban was temporary.
In May 2023 OpenAI released its iOS app and expanded availability to 11 more countries; a New York lawyer was caught citing nonexistent cases ChatGPT invented.

Comedian and author Sara Silverman sued OpenAI over its 'Book2' dataset, and the Authors Guild, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 others, filed a class-action suit in September; much of Silverman's suit was dismissed.
The Associated Press announced in August 2023 a licensing agreement with OpenAI to use AP content to train GPT models.
A Washington Post report in August 2023 found OpenAI's March guardrails against political disinformation weren't being enforced.
On September 25, 2023, OpenAI added voice and image inputs to ChatGPT; an Enterprise version was also launched.
OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman just before Thanksgiving 2023, saying he had not been 'consistently candid'; after 72 hours of chaos and three CEOs in as many days, Altman returned.
OpenAI announced GPTs, customizable single-serving versions of the LLM that anyone can create, and has suggested it may enter the AI chip market; running ChatGPT costs about four cents per query.
